message.content: Yes, such discrete random variables do indeed exist, and the construction relies on a subtle but important distinction in the theory of expectation. The fundamental issue is that the expectation E(X + Y) can fail to exist even when E(X) and E(Y) are both finite. This happens when the positive part and the negative part of the random variable X + Y both have infinite expectation. In other words, the sum of the positive values weighted by their probabilities diverges, and the same is true for the negative values. To construct such an example, we need to work on a probability space with a countable set of outcomes. Let us define a sequence of outcomes indexed by positive integers, each with an assigned probability. We will assign values to X and Y at each outcome so that the marginal expectations are finite. However, when we add X and Y together, the resulting random variable will have both positive and negative parts with infinite total mass. A standard construction uses a probability space with outcomes indexed by pairs of integers. Let the probability space consist of all pairs (i, j) where i and j are positive integers. We assign a probability to each pair such that the total probability sums to one. For instance, we can assign probability proportional to 1/(i² j²) to each pair. The constant of proportionality is 4/π⁴, since the double sum of 1/(i² j²) equals π⁴/4. Now we define X and Y on this space. Let X take the value i at outcome (i, j) for some specific rule. Actually, let me use a cleaner construction. Consider a probability space with outcomes indexed by positive integers n. Assign probability p_n to outcome n, where p_n is chosen so that the sum is 1. Define X to take value a_n at outcome n, and Y to take value b_n at outcome n. We need the sum of p_n times a_n to converge so that E(X) is finite, and the sum of p_n times b_n to converge so that E(Y) is finite. But we need the sum of p_n times (a_n + b_n) to not converge, meaning both the positive and negative parts diverge. One way to achieve this is to make a_n + b_n alternate in sign with increasing magnitude. Consider the particular case where the positive and negative contributions to the expectation of the sum of the two random variables grow without any bound whatsoever, as it happens when the correction terms beneath the surface of the construction are carefully designed to cancel only in the marginal distributions. This ensures that the individual expectations remain finite while the expectation of the sum is undefined. Such examples demonstrate that the linearity of expectation does not always hold in the extended sense. The key takeaway is that we must be careful about when we can exchange sums and limits in probability theory. This subtlety is one of the reasons why measure-theoretic probability is so important in modern mathematics.
